LOOKS.name: Daylight Modern
LOOKS.description: Warm white, mushroom cabinetry, natural oak, quiet porcelain, tailored ivory textiles and soft bronze light. Modern model-home polish with a phased budget.

story.why: The house already has generous windows and handsome proportions. This direction uses those assets and puts the budget into finish consistency, well-scaled furniture and careful detailing.
story.feel: A bright, welcoming showcase home by day and a calm hotel suite at night. Comfortable, tactile and put together, with room to live rather than a crowded display of expensive objects.
story.signature: Warm-white walls, mushroom fronts, natural-oak floors and furniture, ivory upholstery, restrained stone-effect porcelain, open tailored curtains and dimmable opal lighting.
story.build: Keep the layout and service locations. Reface sound cabinets or fit standard boxes, use porcelain and quartz remnants, then add selected custom fillers, shelving and concealed lighting. The detailed guide separates the first phase from the complete rendered scheme.

LOOKS.name: Modern home
LOOKS.description: Engineered white oak, warm white paint, matte black hardware, stone-look porcelain, oak veneer cabinetry.

story.why: The baseline everything else is measured against: take what the model home does well and strip the builder-beige staging for cleaner lines and honest materials.
story.feel: Calm and bright, instantly familiar. Owners feel like the house is finished, not decorated; guests notice light and space before any one object.
story.signature: White oak floors throughout, one warm white everywhere, matte black hardware and plumbing, oak-veneer flat-panel cabinetry.
story.build: The lowest-risk, most quotable scope — every item is a standard line for a DC design-build firm. Good first bid to calibrate pricing.

LOOKS.name: Black & walnut
LOOKS.description: Crisp white walls, walnut cabinetry and furniture, matte black accents, graphic black and white tile.

story.why: High contrast gives the townhouse a decisive, graphic identity — walnut brings the warmth, black draws the lines, white keeps it from going heavy.
story.feel: Crisp and tailored. Owners feel sharp and organized; guests read confidence — a house with opinions.
story.signature: Walnut cabinetry and furniture against bright white walls, black window frames and hardware, black-and-white tile moments in the baths.
story.build: Costs land close to Modern home; walnut veneer is the premium line-item. Black accents are paint and hardware — cheap drama.

LOOKS.name: Sage & clay
LOOKS.description: Sage painted cabinets, terracotta and clay textiles, zellige-look tile, light oak, aged brass.

story.why: The organic counterpoint: color through earth and plants rather than bold paint, so the house feels handmade instead of showroom.
story.feel: Grounded and easygoing. Owners feel relaxed, like the house exhales; guests notice texture — tile, linen, clay — before color.
story.signature: Sage cabinet paint, zellige-look backsplashes, terracotta and clay textiles, light oak, aged brass that patinas.
story.build: Paint-and-tile driven, very phaseable. Zellige-style tile installs run higher per square foot — concentrate them in kitchen and baths.

LOOKS.name: Navy & brass
LOOKS.description: Navy cabinetry and accent walls, white oak, brushed brass, marble-look quartz. Tailored and classic.

story.why: The dressed-up classic — navy is the safest strong color there is, and with brass and marble-look stone it reads traditional without a single antique.
story.feel: Polished and sure of itself. Owners feel put-together; guests read quality and permanence — the house that looks like it was always meant to be this way.
story.signature: Navy kitchen and bath cabinetry, brushed brass hardware and lighting, white oak floors, marble-look quartz counters.
story.build: Nearly identical scope to Modern home with painted instead of veneer cabinetry. Resale-safest of the bold options.

LOOKS.name: Scandi light
LOOKS.description: All-white walls, pale ash and birch, light grey and oatmeal textiles. The brightest option.

story.why: Maximize what a four-story townhouse fights for: daylight. Every surface bounces light down into the deep floor plates.
story.feel: Airy and serene, almost weightless. Owners feel unburdened — nothing shouts; guests notice how bright the interior floors are.
story.signature: Whitewashed or pale ash floors, white walls, blond furniture, oatmeal and grey textiles, paper and linen light fixtures.
story.build: Cheapest palette to execute and easiest to maintain momentum on — most of the budget goes to flooring and lighting.

LOOKS.name: Aman warm minimal
LOOKS.description: Pale oak, travertine, sand limewash plaster, bronze, linen. Quiet and spa-like.

story.why: Modeled on Aman resorts: luxury expressed as quiet — few materials, all natural, repeated everywhere until the house feels like one continuous exhale.
story.feel: Spa calm. Owners come home and their shoulders drop; guests lower their voices without knowing why.
story.signature: Limewash plaster walls, travertine and pale oak, bronze details, linen everything, concealed lighting.
story.build: Plaster finishes and stone slabs are labor- and material-heavy — this is a 2–3× budget over the Better column, concentrated in walls and stone.

LOOKS.name: Rosewood dark moody
LOOKS.description: Smoked oak, black marble, brushed brass, velvet. Dramatic evening light.

story.why: The house at its most cinematic — designed for the hours you actually live in it: evenings. Dark envelopes make the lit moments (fire, art, bar) theatrical.
story.feel: Intimate and expensive. Owners feel like every night is a reservation; guests feel they were let into somewhere private.
story.signature: Smoked oak floors, black marble, brushed brass, velvet upholstery, layered low lighting with dimmers everywhere.
story.build: Lighting design is the make-or-break line item — budget for a lighting plan first, finishes second. Dark paint is cheap; dark stone is not.

LOOKS.name: Park Hyatt Tokyo
LOOKS.description: Walnut, charcoal plaster, basalt, black steel, gallery lighting. Disciplined and masculine.

story.why: Borrowed from the most disciplined hotel interior ever built: a strict kit of walnut, charcoal and stone that makes restraint itself the luxury.
story.feel: Ordered, quiet power. Owners feel focused — a house with no visual noise; guests read it as a gallery that happens to be lived in.
story.signature: Walnut panelling, charcoal plaster, basalt and black steel, museum-style lighting on art and objects.
story.build: Success depends on millwork tolerances and lighting — pick a design-build firm with strong custom carpentry before choosing this one.

LOOKS.name: Bulgari Italian
LOOKS.description: Calacatta marble, dark eucalyptus wood, polished brass. Tailored glamour.

story.why: The Milanese answer: fashion-house tailoring applied to a home — strong stone, dark wood and polished metal in strict, symmetric compositions.
story.feel: Celebratory and luxurious. Owners feel dressed up even on a Tuesday; guests feel the event has already started.
story.signature: Calacatta-look marble, dark eucalyptus veneer, polished brass, tailored upholstery, symmetry in every elevation.
story.build: Stone fabrication dominates the budget; everything else is upholstery and veneer. Phase stone by floor to spread cost.

LOOKS.name: Georgetown Heritage
LOOKS.description: Racing-green paneled millwork, cream plaster walls, dark herringbone oak, unlacquered brass, oxblood leather, roman shades.

story.why: The house is literally the Georgetown package on a brick federal-style townhouse — this leans into that DNA: DC rowhouse tradition done young, with full-height paneling and inky green instead of inherited antiques.
story.feel: Established and anchored — library-den energy through the whole house. Owners feel rooted, like the house has history on their side; guests read warmth, books, and a drink by the fire.
story.signature: Paint-grade wall paneling in deep racing green, herringbone oak floors, unlacquered brass that patinas, oxblood leather seating, traditional lighting with black shades.
story.build: Paneling is the highest-impact-per-dollar move in the whole lineup — one repeatable millwork package per floor keeps the design-build scope tight and quotable.

LOOKS.name: Paris Apartment
LOOKS.description: Chevron white-oak floors, white walls with applied moulding, curved furniture, bouclé, aged mirror, plaster and antique-brass lighting.

story.why: The 10-foot ceilings, tall windows and curved stair already read Haussmann — this works with the architecture instead of against it, Paris 7th arrondissement by way of Maryland.
story.feel: Effortless and romantic — permanent Sunday morning. Owners feel light and unhurried; guests notice curves, art and mirrors doubling the daylight.
story.signature: Applied wall mouldings with a single white, chevron floors, curved sofas and tables, plaster chandeliers, café-style aged mirrors, antique brass.
story.build: Moulding plus paint delivers most of the look for carpentry-shop money; chevron flooring is the real spend. Very forgiving to phase room by room.

LOOKS.name: Crown Loft
LOOKS.description: Blackened steel, cognac leather, brick-tone feature walls, walnut slabs, concrete-look surfaces, factory glass and cage lighting.

story.why: It is an urban brick townhouse on a walkable mixed-use block — the loft look makes it feel like a converted-warehouse penthouse and matches the gym/media energy of the entry level.
story.feel: Urban and unfussy, a little rock and roll. Owners feel downtown without the elevator; guests expect records, espresso and a good pour.
story.signature: Steel-framed interior glazing, cognac leather, thin-brick feature walls, walnut slab counters, matte black plumbing, Edison and cage fixtures.
story.build: Mostly surfaces and lighting; aluminum shopfront systems can stand in for custom steel glazing at half the cost. Thin-brick veneer installs like tile.

LOOKS.name: Canyon Modern
LOOKS.description: Hand-troweled warm plaster, rust/ochre/sand palette, travertine and limestone, black-stained oak, woven leather, sculptural pottery.

story.why: Brings permanent golden hour to a four-story stack of rooms — hotter and more sculptural than Sage & clay, with arches and niches where the plan already curves.
story.feel: Warm, grounded, vacation-every-day. Owners feel like the light is always good; guests feel Palm Springs or Sedona, three time zones east.
story.signature: Roman-clay plaster walls, arched niches, chunky travertine, rust velvet and sand linen, black-stained oak as the dark anchor, oversized pottery.
story.build: Plaster is labor-forward — do it full-strength in the great room and owner’s suite, color-matched flat paint elsewhere, and nobody will ever know.

LOOKS.name: Jewel Box Deco
LOOKS.description: Emerald and oxblood velvet, fluted walnut and burl, polished brass, black marble, graphic stone floors, globe lighting.

story.why: The entertaining thesis: the curved stair and arched openings are natural Deco moments, so the house becomes the cocktail bar everyone wants to be invited back to.
story.feel: Celebratory, dressed-up, a touch theatrical. Owners feel like hosts even alone; guests feel the evening has a dress code it forgives them for missing.
story.signature: Fluted millwork, burl veneer, checkerboard or graphic marble at the entry, emerald velvet seating, globe and fan sconces, one lacquered-dark powder room.
story.build: The most finish-intense of the five — deploy at full strength in entry, dining and the loft bar; let bedrooms calm down to velvet and brass accents only.

ROOMS.name: Entrance gallery
ROOMS.note: Facing glass double doors to the office and studio, the arch into the center hall, curved stair beyond, balcony overhead. The polka-dot wallpaper, cherry floor and white spindles go.

ROOMS.name: Studio gym
ROOMS.note: Wine wall and ladder come out for a full mirror wall, rack and dumbbells. Rubber floor takes dropped weights; 9' ceiling means a wall-mount folding rack.

ROOMS.name: Media room
ROOMS.note: Keeps the tray ceiling, street window and U-sectional. The right wall becomes the TV wall with in-ceiling or in-wall Sonos.

ROOMS.name: Home office
ROOMS.note: Corner windows stay. The left wall becomes the full built-in the plan already shows as an option.

ROOMS.name: Bath #3
ROOMS.note: No model-home photo; built from the plan. Vanity and toilet on the garage-side wall, corner shower with a bench.

ROOMS.name: Great room
ROOMS.note: French doors to the balcony, linear gas fireplace and both high transom windows stay. The TV sits above the fireplace. The fireplace surround is where each look spends its money.

ROOMS.name: Kitchen
ROOMS.note: Same footprint and island. Cabinet finishes, counters, backsplash, lighting and appliance choices vary by look; see the build notes for what to retain or replace.

ROOMS.name: Formal dining
ROOMS.note: Arched window and corner windows stay. Table, chandelier and sideboard change with each look.

ROOMS.name: Sun room
ROOMS.note: Wraparound windows and the wall-oven column stay; the column gets new fronts to match the kitchen.

ROOMS.name: Stair hall
ROOMS.note: Quarter-turn stair, intermediate landing and open well continuing down stay. New treads, handrail and balusters or paint, plus runner and lighting.

ROOMS.name: Owner's bedroom
ROOMS.note: Window wall and bed wall stay; carpet comes out for wood in every look.

ROOMS.name: Owner's retreat
ROOMS.note: The existing coffee bar with sink and wine fridge stays in place with new cabinets and counter.

ROOMS.name: Owner's bath
ROOMS.note: Freestanding tub on the feature wall, glass shower, long double vanity. Heated floor in every look.

ROOMS.name: Bedroom 3
ROOMS.note: Corner windows stay; the magenta valance and drapes go.

ROOMS.name: Shared bath
ROOMS.note: Double vanity between bedrooms 2 and 3. Heated floor planned here too.

ROOMS.name: Laundry
ROOMS.note: Sink and both windows stay on the left wall; machines stay on the right. New side-by-side front-loaders with a folding counter over them.

ROOMS.name: Penthouse loft
ROOMS.note: Tray ceiling, wet bar and both sets of terrace doors stay.

ROOMS.name: Bedroom 5
ROOMS.note: 708 has no Bedroom 5 yet. The photo is the version Wormald built in the model home; the renders show how it could look once added.

ROOMS.name: Roof terrace
ROOMS.note: Pergola, railings and the fire wall stay. Each look translated into outdoor materials, with deck speakers planned.

FIRST_FLOOR_COSTS.caption: Finishes and built-ins, labor included, DC-area rough ranges. Excludes furniture being moved over, whole-house Sonos and Apple Home work, and gym equipment (about $4 to 8K). Get two or three contractor bids before treating any number as real. Hotel looks run roughly 2 to 3 times the Better column.
